content.text: A column can be perfectly true in your historical table and still be unknown at the moment the model has to decide. If it's written because of the outcome, the model learns it as a shortcut, cross-validation approves it, and production breaks it. For every feature, ask what its value was at prediction time.

A subscription app trains a churn model on last quarter's customers. The data team exports one row per customer, every column the warehouse has, and the model scores a cross-validated AUC of 0.949. A month after launch, the retention team reports that the weekly list of at-risk customers is nearly empty. The model now catches 4% of the customers who leave. Its strongest feature was "received a retention call", and the retention team only calls customers who have already asked to cancel.
The common misconception
Many developers treat the historical table as the feature set: if a column is in the data and it predicts the label, it's fair game. It's an easy belief to hold:

items.text: The data is real. Every value was really recorded; nothing was invented or copied from the label column.
Validation approves it. Cross-validation and the test set both reward the column, so it looks like signal.
The rule everyone learns is about rows: keep the test rows out of training. Nobody says anything about columns.

content.text: The half-truth: every value in the table is true. But it's true as of the day you exported it, not as of the moment your model will be asked to decide.
What actually happens

A prediction happens at a point in time: when a customer opens the app, when a loan application arrives, when a patient is admitted. A feature is legitimate only if, at that moment, its value already exists and equals the value you trained on. Google's Machine Learning Crash Course puts it as a rule: during training, use only the features you'll have available when serving. Breaking it is
target leakage
, also called label leakage: information about the label reaching the model through a feature.
The model takes the shortcut

A column written because of the outcome is the easiest pattern in the data, so the model leans on it. The script rebuilds the churn story. Three honest features carry a weak signal; the fourth records a retention call, made for 80% of the customers who cancelled. The model trains on 4,000 customers, and the other 2,000 play live traffic. At prediction time nobody has cancelled yet, so for them the call column is 0 for everyone, as it would be in production.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(6000, 3))  # tenure, monthly bill, support tickets
y = rng.random(6000) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(1.5 - X @ [-0.8, 0.5, 0.7]))
called = y & (rng.random(6000) < 0.8)  # retention calls cancellers
X_export = np.column_stack([X, called])  # exported after the quarter
X_live = np.column_stack([X, np.zeros(6000)])  # nobody has cancelled yet

model = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0)
auc = cross_val_score(model, X_export[:4000], y[:4000], cv=5,
                      scoring="roc_auc").mean()
print(f"cross-validated AUC {auc:.3f}")
proba = model.fit(X_export[:4000], y[:4000]).predict_proba(X_live[4000:])
live_auc = roc_auc_score(y[4000:], proba[:, 1])
live_recall = recall_score(y[4000:], proba[:, 1] >= 0.5)
print(f"live AUC {live_auc:.3f}, recall {live_recall:.3f}")
# cross-validated AUC 0.949
# live AUC 0.715, recall 0.043

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(6000, 3))  # known before anyone cancels
y = rng.random(6000) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(1.5 - X @ [-0.8, 0.5, 0.7]))
# the retention call happens after the outcome: not a feature

model = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0)
auc = cross_val_score(model, X[:4000], y[:4000], cv=5,
                      scoring="roc_auc").mean()
print(f"cross-validated AUC {auc:.3f}")
proba = model.fit(X[:4000], y[:4000]).predict_proba(X[4000:])
live_auc = roc_auc_score(y[4000:], proba[:, 1])
live_recall = recall_score(y[4000:], proba[:, 1] >= 0.5)
print(f"live AUC {live_auc:.3f}, recall {live_recall:.3f}")
# cross-validated AUC 0.745
# live AUC 0.738, recall 0.277

content.text: ROC AUC

measures how well the model ranks churners above loyal customers: 0.5 is a random order, 1.0 is perfect. The leaky model reports 0.949. On live data it ranks at 0.715 and catches 4.3% of churners at the default cutoff, because it learned that "no call" means "probably staying", and in production nobody has had a call. The honest model reports a modest 0.745 and delivers 0.738, catching 27.7%. Its cross-validation predicted production; the leaky one's didn't. The leaky model even ranks worse, because it spent its effort on the shortcut instead of the real signals.
Why cross-validation can't see it

The leak lives in a column, so it's in every row of every fold: training and validation rows were exported the same way, after the outcome. Cross-validation measures how well the model generalizes to new rows from the same table. It can't tell you whether the table matches the world at prediction time. Kapoor and Narayanan list illegitimate features as their own category in a taxonomy of leakage, and note that judging legitimacy takes domain knowledge, so they ask researchers to justify every feature instead.
Three shapes of leakage

items.text: The retention call. Kapoor and Narayanan cite a study that used anti-hypertensive drug use to predict hypertension. The Crash Course describes a cancer model that leaned on hospital names, because some hospitals specialize in cancer; at inference the hospital wasn't known yet.

"Days since last login", "account status" or "lifetime spend" read from today's tables for last year's rows. Rule #31 of Google's Rules of ML warns that a table you join at training and serving time may change in between.

In civil war prediction, one paper used several variables that were proxies for civil war itself and reached near-perfect accuracy. Corrected, no model beat a baseline that predicted the previous year's outcome.

content.text: When one column carries most of the score, find out who writes it and when. scikit-learn's
permutation_importance
shows how much the score drops when a column is shuffled. A single feature that beats a reasonable domain baseline by a wide margin deserves suspicion before celebration.

A leaked feature usually still exists at serving time: it's just 0, empty or stale. The model keeps returning probabilities, the dashboards stay green, and the predictions quietly lose their value. Only checking live outcomes, or the feature's values at serving time against training, will reveal it.
How to apply it in your project
Write down exactly when the model is called and what the system knows at that instant.
For each feature, record who writes it, when, and whether it can change after the prediction moment.

items.title: Build features as of a cutoff

content.text: Compute each row's features from events before its prediction time, not from current tables.
Train on earlier periods and evaluate on later ones, with features rebuilt as of each prediction date.
Rule #29 of the Rules of ML: log the features at serving time and use those logs for training.
Key takeaways

items.text: A feature is legitimate only if its value exists, unchanged, at the moment of prediction.
The leaky churn model scored 0.949 in cross-validation and caught 4.3% of churners live.
Cross-validation can't detect target leakage: the leak is in every fold.
Audit columns by when they're written, build features as of a cutoff, and validate on later data.
